items.title: Classification by GFR and albuminuria
items.contentHtml:
Classification by GFR and albuminuria

  • Chronic kidney disease is classified according to the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in stages: G1 (GFR ≥90 ml/min/1.73m²), G2 (GFR 60-89), G3a (GFR 45-59), G3b (GFR 30-44), G4 (GFR 15-29) and G5 (GFR <15).
  • Albuminuria is categorized into A1 (<30 mg/g creatinine), A2 (30-300 mg/g) and A3 (>300 mg/g).
  • The risk of progression and complications is determined by combining stage G and category A, according to the KDIGO guidelines.
  • The Albuminuria is a marker of kidney damage and a predictor of cardiovascular events, independently of GFR.

items.foco: Most frequent causes: diabetes and HTN
items.title: Most frequent causes
items.contentHtml:
Most frequent causes: diabetes and high blood pressure

  • Diabetes mellitus is the main cause of chronic kidney disease in the world, responsible for up to 40% of incident cases in dialysis.
  • High blood pressure is the second most common cause; strict control of blood pressure (<130/80 mmHg) delays progression.
  • Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by persistent albuminuria and progressive decrease in GFR; Intensive glycemic control reduces the risk of microalbuminuria.
  • In arterial hypertension, nephroangiosclerosis produces glomerular ischemic damage; inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system are the first line for nephroprotection.

items.title: Referral to nephrology
items.contentHtml:
Criteria for referral to nephrology

  • Nephrology should be referred when the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is <30 ml/min/1.73m² (stage G4 or G5).
  • Also when there is a rapid decrease in GFR (>5 ml/min/1.73m²/year) or a significant increase in albuminuria (>300 mg/g).
  • Other indications: nephrotic proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), persistent glomerular hematuria, arterial hypertension that is difficult to control, suspicion of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
  • Early referral improves the planning of renal replacement therapy and reduces mortality associated with chronic kidney disease.

items.title: Anemia due to erythropoietin deficiency
items.contentHtml:
Anemia due to erythropoietin deficiency

  • Anemia in chronic kidney disease is normocytic, normochromic, due to a deficiency in renal production of erythropoietin.
  • Treatment with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (e.g. epoetin alfa) is initiated when hemoglobin is <10 g/dL, adjusting to maintain between 10-12 g/dL.
  • Before starting, other causes must be ruled out: iron deficiency, vitamin B12, folic acid, occult bleeding and inflammation.
  • Intravenous iron (iron saccharate) is the first line if transferrin saturation is <30% or ferritin <200 ng/mL.

items.title: Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
items.contentHtml:
Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis

  • Hyperkalemia (potassium >5.5 mEq/L) in chronic kidney disease is due to decreased renal excretion and use of drugs such as inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
  • Acute management: intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize cardiac membrane, insulin + glucose, beta-agonists inhalants and exchange resins (e.g. sodium polystyrene sulfonate).
  • Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) is common when GFR <30 ml/min; serum bicarbonate should be maintained >22 mEq/L.
  • Treatment with oral sodium bicarbonate (0.5-1 mEq/kg/day) slows the progression of chronic kidney disease and improves nutritional status.

items.title: Indications for urgent dialysis
items.contentHtml:
Indications for urgent dialysis

  • The absolute indications for urgent dialysis are: severe hyperkalemia (>6.5 mEq/L) with electrocardiographic changes, severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) refractory to medical treatment, acute pulmonary edema resistant to diuretics.
  • Other indications: uremic pericarditis (pericardial rub, chest pain), uremic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, seizures), gastrointestinal bleeding due to uremic platelet dysfunction.
  • In uremic syndrome, serum urea >200 mg/dL usually accompanies clinical indications.
  • Emergency peritoneal dialysis is contraindicated. if there is recent abdominal surgery or active peritonitis.

items.title: Bone mineral disorder
items.contentHtml:
Management of bone mineral disorder

  • The bone mineral disorder of chronic kidney disease is characterized by alterations in calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D.
  • Serum phosphorus should be maintained between 2.5-4.5 mg/dL; if it is elevated, dietary restriction and phosphorus chelators (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum) are indicated.
  • The intact PTH should be maintained between 2-9 times the normal value depending on the stage; if it is elevated, vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, paricalcitol) or calcimimetics (cinacalcet) are used.
  • Avoid hypercalcemia with calcium chelators; In stage G5, sevelamer or lanthanum is preferred to avoid vascular calcification.

items.title: Calculation of GFR by CKD-EPI
items.contentHtml:
Calculation of GFR by CKD-EPI

  • The CKD-EPI equation (Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration) estimates the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in ml/min/1.73m², being more precise than MDRD in GFR >60.
  • It is based on serum creatinine, age, sex and race (African American or not).
  • The formula is: GFR = 141 × min(Cr/κ, 1)^α × max(Cr/κ, 1)^(-1.209) × 0.993^age × (1.018 if female) × (1.159 if black race), where κ=0.7 (female) or 0.9 (male), α=-0.329 (woman) or -0.411 (man).
  • To report, round to the nearest integer; Values ​​>90 are not reported as exact but as '≥90'.

items.title: Prevention of contrast nephrotoxicity
items.contentHtml:
Prevention of contrast nephrotoxicity

  • Contrast nephropathy is defined as an increase in serum creatinine >0.3 mg/dL or >50% of baseline within 48-72 hours after administration of iodinated contrast.
  • The main preventive measure is intravenous hydration with isotonic saline solution (1 ml/kg/hour) 12 hours before and after the procedure.
  • In patients with GFR <30 ml/min/1.73m², iodinated contrast should be avoided if possible; if essential, use isoosmolar contrast and minimal volume.
  • N-acetylcysteine (600 mg every 12 hours, orally, before and after) has controversial evidence; it is not universally recommended as a standard.

items.title: Drug dosage adjustment
items.contentHtml:
Drug dose adjustment

  • In chronic kidney disease, renal elimination of drugs is reduced; the dose should be adjusted according to the estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
  • High-risk drugs: metformin (contraindicated if GFR <30 ml/min), direct anticoagulants (dabigatran contraindicated if GFR <30), aminoglycosides (adjustment by GFR and monitoring of levels).
  • Inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system are maintained up to GFR >15 ml/min, but require monitoring of potassium and creatinine.
  • Opioids such as morphine have active metabolites that accumulate; Fentanyl or hydromorphone with range adjustment is preferred.

items.title: Nutrition: protein and potassium restriction
items.contentHtml:
Nutrition: protein and potassium restriction

  • Protein restriction to 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day in patients with GFR <30 ml/min slows the progression of chronic kidney disease and reduces uremia.
  • Potassium intake should be limited to <2-3 g/day in hyperkalemia or GFR <30, avoiding rich foods: banana, orange, tomato, potatoes, legumes.
  • Phosphorus is restricted to <800 mg/day when PTH is elevated or serum phosphorus >4.5 mg/dL.
  • It is recommended supplementation of water-soluble vitamins (B1, B6, B12, folic acid) and avoidance of vitamin A supplements due to risk of toxicity.

items.title: Uremic syndrome and pericarditis
items.contentHtml:
Uremic syndrome and pericarditis

  • The uremic syndrome is the set of symptoms and signs due to the accumulation of uremic toxins when the GFR <15 ml/min: nausea, anorexia, pruritus, asterixis, peripheral neuropathy, seizures.
  • The uremic pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium due to chemical irritation in uremia; It presents with pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub and low fever.
  • On the electrocardiogram there may be diffuse elevation of the ST segment; The echocardiogram rules out pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade.
  • Treatment is urgent dialysis (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis); Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are contraindicated due to the risk of bleeding.
